title: The Fed Is Off Its Own Reaction Function. It Should Tell Us Why.
gist: Jason Furman shows the Fed's dots work as a Taylor-rule reaction function to its own forecast revisions (R-squared 0.77), but that the Fed is now 1.15 points below it (1.85 implied vs 0.7 delivered on the end-2026 rate, to 4.1 percent) after core PCE projection rose from 2.5 to 3.4 percent. He argues the gap may reflect wisdom, since tariff and Iran-conflict inflation is transitory and trimmed-mean/median measures are falling, and urges the Fed to publish rule readings and explain deviations.

insights.claim: The Fed's rate projections are poor predictions of its own policy path: of 51 sets of projections since 2012 scored against the set a year later, rates ended higher than projected 15 times and lower 21 times, with the rest mostly zero-rate years.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Do not trade the dots as a plan; treat them as conditional on data.
insights.locator: The Fed's Economic Projections as a Reaction Function

insights.claim: The dots should be read as a conditional reaction function, not a plan: the Fed says how much it expects to move rates but will adjust if inflation or unemployment depart from its forecast.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Rate-path surprises are mostly forecast-error pass-through, so trade the data surprise, not the dot.
insights.quote: the projections not as a plan for its actions but as setting out a reaction function

insights.claim: Large historical misses were consistent with a Taylor rule on the Fed's own forecast revisions: in December 2018 the Fed projected two hikes for 2019 but cut three times (a swing of about 1.25 points), matching a rule-implied 0.6 + 0.4 + 0.3 = 1.3 points once core PCE came in 0.4 lower, unemployment 0.1 higher and neutral estimates fell.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Past dovish pivots were rule-consistent, not discretionary.
insights.locator: Take two examples

insights.claim: In 2022 the Fed raised rates by 4.25 points against a December 2021 plan of 0.75; about 3 of the 3.5-point overage is explained by the Taylor rule applied to core PCE coming in at 4.8 percent rather than the forecast 2.7.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: The 2022 hiking shock was largely the reaction function operating on an inflation miss.
insights.locator: In December 2021

insights.claim: A Taylor rule in changes applied to the Fed's own forecast revisions explains about 77 percent of the variation in how the Fed moves its year-end rate projection, with a typical miss of 0.66 points versus 1.22 for assuming no change; free-fit weights are 1.57 on inflation and 0.99 on unemployment, close to Taylor's 1.5 and 1.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Gives a quantitative tool to estimate where the Fed should move given data surprises.
insights.locator: Figure 1

insights.claim: The committee reacts to its inflation forecast rather than trailing twelve-month inflation: a rule in changes run on realized data explains nothing (R-squared 0.00) over 2012-26, while the forecast-revision version explains 0.77.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Forward inflation expectations in the SEP, not trailing prints, drive Fed moves.
insights.locator: Finally, the weights (Table A3)

themes.theme: Fed far below its reaction function now

insights.claim: Since December 2025 the Fed's forecasts have shifted by enough that its own reaction function calls for raising the end-2026 funds rate path by 1.85 points to about 5.25 percent, yet it raised it only 0.7 to 4.1 percent, a shortfall of 1.15 points.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Market pricing near 4.1 percent sits well below what a rules-based Fed would deliver, a tail risk for hawkish repricing.
insights.locator: The Federal Funds Rate Is Currently Well Below

insights.claim: The Fed's core PCE inflation projection for 2026 rose from 2.5 percent in December 2025 to 3.4 percent in September 2026, which alone would justify a 1.35 point hike under a Taylor rule, versus a 0.25 point hike delivered and about 0.5 points priced by the market for 2026.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Inflation surprise is the main source of the policy gap.
insights.locator: The bigger, and less pleasant, surprise

insights.claim: The Fed's unemployment projection for end-2026 fell from 4.4 percent to 4.1 percent, enough under a Taylor reaction function to eliminate the 25 basis point cut planned in December 2025.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Labor-market strength removes the easing case.
insights.locator: The Federal Funds Rate Is Currently Well Below

insights.claim: The current dovish deviation from the reaction function ranks among the most extreme on record: of 37 comparable twelve-month readings since 2012, only five were more dovish and all five came in the past three years.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: The Fed has been persistently looser than its rule for three years, which is a regime feature.
insights.locator: only five have been more dovish

insights.claim: The shortfall is not tied to the current Chair: anchoring on the March 2026 projections, the last under Powell, the rule implies a 1.45 point increase since March against 0.7 delivered, a 0.75 point gap; earlier rounds since September 2023 imply on average a rate about 1.3 points above the Fed's current 4.1 percent.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: The dovish gap persists across leadership, so it is not a Warsh-specific story.
insights.locator: This is not just about the current Chair

insights.claim: The case that the Fed is wise to deviate is that part of the inflation comes from tariffs and the Iran conflict, which raise the price level once and then stop adding to inflation, so the Fed should not react to them as it would not react to a VAT increase.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Tariff pass-through is a one-time level shift, supporting a patient Fed if it holds.
insights.locator: Another interpretation is that the Fed is wiser than the formula

insights.claim: To justify switching from a planned 25 basis point cut to the 50 basis points of hikes priced by the market, the Fed's inputs would need to be unemployment of 4.2 percent and core PCE inflation of about 2.7 percent, roughly half a point below a reasonable current forecast of about 3.2 percent that could be attributed to transitory factors.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: The Fed is implicitly discounting about 0.5 points of inflation as transitory; failure of that bet means more hikes.
insights.locator: Quantification can shed some light

insights.claim: Core PCE inflation has diverged from underlying measures: from July 2025 to July 2026 core PCE rose from 2.8 to 3.0 percent while the Dallas Fed trimmed mean fell from 2.8 to 2.3 and the Cleveland Fed median from 3.5 to 2.7; treating the gap as noise puts the Fed roughly on its reaction function.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Trimmed-mean and median trends are the evidence for the Fed's looking-through story.
insights.locator: Table A4

insights.claim: With the trimmed-mean adjustment the rule's implied 1.85 point increase becomes 0.9, and with the median adjustment 0.6, against the 0.7 the Fed actually did, so the apparent policy gap depends heavily on which inflation measure is used.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Whether the Fed is off course hinges on choice of core versus trimmed or median inflation.
insights.locator: Table A4

insights.claim: Furman began the exercise believing the Fed was well off base but after quantifying it ended up more sympathetic to its approach.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: A prominent critic-leaning economist sees the Fed's looseness as defensible.
insights.quote: I confess, I began this exercise thinking the Fed was way off base

insights.claim: Level-based Taylor-type rules have placed the funds rate below the rule at most meetings since 2012, by 1.3 to 2.7 points on average depending mainly on the neutral rate used, so persistent apparent dovishness against levels rules is normal for the period.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: A level gap alone is not a signal; the claim concerns the Fed's own reaction function.
insights.locator: Table A2

insights.claim: Today's funds rate gap to the Taylor (1993) rule of 1.5 points is only at the 38th percentile of meetings since 1990, about as far below the rule as is normal.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Rules in levels do not flag the Fed as unusually loose now.
insights.locator: By any of these level measures

insights.claim: Inertial and first-difference rules track the funds rate closely (mean gaps -0.1 and -0.3 points) only by construction, since they start from the current rate, so they describe persistence rather than where the rate should be.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Good fit of inertial rules is uninformative for judging policy stance.
insights.locator: Table A2

insights.claim: Giving unemployment the balanced-approach weight of 2 instead of 1 fits the Fed's moves worse on every sample (R-squared 0.71 versus 0.77).
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: The Fed's revealed reaction is closer to Taylor 1993 than the balanced-approach rule.
insights.locator: Table A1

insights.claim: Realized-data rules fail because 2012-26 policy was driven by levels: liftoff on a schedule in 2015-18, catch-up of more than four points in 2022-23 while trailing core inflation was already falling, then normalization from a restrictive level.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Backward-looking inflation rules misread Fed behavior in catch-up periods.
insights.locator: The same rule in changes run on the realized data

insights.claim: Furman wants the Fed to publish the Taylor rule recommendation at every rate-setting meeting rather than only twice a year in the Monetary Policy Report, ideally picking one main reference rule.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Possible policy change that would make deviations from rule more visible to markets.
insights.quote: I would like to see the Fed publish the Taylor rule recommendation at every one of its rate-setting meetings

insights.claim: A reaction function expressed as a path plus an explanation of how it will adjust with inflation and unemployment surprises is preferable, though it risks perpetuating and compounding errors over time.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Path-plus-adjustment communication is better but not error-free.
insights.locator: The Bottom Line

insights.claim: The Fed should explicitly say it is discounting about half a point of the inflation forecast error as transitory and will make up for it with further hikes if wrong, because policymakers and staff know more than the formula and should convey it.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Unexplained deviation risks credibility; explicit transitory discount creates a testable commitment.
insights.locator: In the current situation that could take the form

insights.claim: On current trajectory the Fed has gone from planning one 25 basis point cut this year to being on track for two increases, because unemployment has been lower and inflation higher than expected.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: The policy direction has flipped from easing to tightening within the year.
insights.locator: We were planning one 25 basis point rate cut
